item.title: Microsoft Entra Connect Health Breach Exposes Tenant Metadata and Admin Details
item.description:
Microsoft Entra Connect Health breach exposed tenant metadata and admin details, potentially enabling targeted phishing and social-engineering attacks.

Microsoft has disclosed a data breach involving its Entra Connect Health service, which exposed tenant metadata and administrator contact details.

“On 9 November 2026, we detected a vulnerability in the Microsoft Entra Connect Health API that was introduced on 23 July 2026. The vulnerability could allow an unauthorized party to access tenant and service-monitoring metadata and potentially make changes to Connect Health monitoring configuration.” the company wrote on Reddit.

Microsoft Entra Connect Health is a cloud service that helps administrators monitor the health, performance and alerts of their on-premises identity systems. The IT giant says no passwords, authentication tokens or valid cryptographic keys were compromised, but the exposed information could still help attackers craft convincing phishing and social-engineering attacks.

The issue came from a vulnerability in the Entra Connect Health API, introduced on July 23, 2026. Microsoft identified the flaw on November 9 and deployed a server-side fix on November 19.

“We deployed and fixed the vulnerability on 19 November 2026. On 20 November 2026, we concluded our investigation and determined that unauthorized read-only access to tenant-level metadata associated with your organization had occurred. We did not identify any unauthorized configuration changes.” the IT giant added.

Customers do not need to install a software update because Microsoft addressed the problem on its side.

The attackers could only view the data, but the exposure still created risks. They gained access to administrator email addresses, tenant IDs, domain names and synchronisation status. Attackers could use this information to plan targeted attacks and impersonate Microsoft support staff, service providers or internal IT administrators.

Microsoft has not disclosed how many tenants were affected. However, several administrators and managed service providers have reported receiving notifications from the company, suggesting that the breach may have affected many customers.

Microsoft says no software update or customer remediation is needed because the Entra Connect Health API vulnerability has been fixed. However, it recommends several precautionary steps. Organisations should alert security and IT teams to possible targeted phishing and social-engineering attempts, ensure administrator accounts use phishing-resistant MFA, and apply Privileged Identity Management for just-in-time access.

They should also run Microsoft’s read-only PowerShell script to review potentially exposed metadata, check Connect Health settings, and examine Entra audit logs, sign-in logs and Azure Activity Logs for suspicious activity. Microsoft advises verifying the security notice directly through Azure Service Health rather than clicking email links.

item.title: Cleverbridge Confirms Attackers Copied Payment Card Data From Its Platform
item.description:
Cleverbridge confirms attackers stole payment card numbers, expiry dates and CVV codes, warning customers to watch for fraudulent transactions.

Cleverbridge, which runs checkouts, payments and subscriptions for other companies, has confirmed that attackers copied payment card data from its platform. The company says it found the problem on 4 November and started notifying affected people on 20 November. That’s a gap of 16 days.

“On 4 November 2026, Cleverbridge detected unauthorised activity in our platform and took immediate steps to contain the incident.” reads the incident update published by the company. “Whilst our investigation remains ongoing, regretfully, we have been able to determine that a third party copied payment card data stored on our platform.”

Affected systems went offline for a short time and were back online the same day. Only later did the investigation show that a third party had copied payment card data stored on the platform, and the company says that the investigation is still running.

The company’s website lists customers such as SUSE, Red Hat and Parallels, but the company has not said which businesses were affected.

If you bought a product or service from a company that uses Cleverbridge, it may have handled your payment and stored your card details. Cleverbridge provides payment and subscription services to software and SaaS companies.

Cleverbridge has not clearly explained what information was stolen on its public incident page. It says the exposed data may include payment card details and directs affected customers to check their individual notifications. However, a notification reviewed by BleepingComputer provides more details: the stolen information may include card numbers, expiration dates and CVV or CVC security codes.

That last item is the one that matters. The card industry’s own rules generally bar companies from keeping the security code once a payment is authorised, so BleepingComputer asked Cleverbridge why the codes were accessible at all.

The company did not disclose technical details about the attack, however, its answer excluded a ransomware attack.

“None of our systems were encrypted.” continues the update.

Cleverbridge says it hired TransUnion/Cyberscout, a third-party vendor, to support the notifications, and that a notice sent on its behalf is legitimate. It has offered credit or identity monitoring where available, with sign-up details in the notice. Asked why people weren’t told sooner, it says it moved fast and notified them without undue delay.

Cleverbridge advises users to watch for phishing attempts and warns that it will never request card details, passwords or security codes by email, phone or text.

“As always, we recommend that our users follow general best online security practices, remain vigilant, and be aware of phishing attempts.” the company states. “Out of an abundance of caution, please be cautious of unexpected emails, calls, or messages about this incident. Cleverbridge will never ask you for your card details, passwords, or security codes by email, phone, or text message. ”

Call your card issuer sooner rather than later. Cleverbridge says the issuer may decide to replace your card after you report the incident.

We recommend that you check your card statements carefully and tell your card issuer right away about any transaction that you do not recognise.” concludes the report. “You may also wish to contact your card issuer to tell them about this incident and follow any advice they give, as they may decide to replace your card. ”

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, payment card data)

item.title: Hackers May Have Breached FBI Database Used by Police Nationwide
item.description:
FBI investigates an apparent breach of its NCIC criminal database, raising concerns over sensitive law enforcement data and security.

The FBI is investigating a possible breach of a database that police use to check arrest warrants and access criminal records. According to the BBC, US media reported the incident, citing two people familiar with the matter. The FBI has not publicly commented on the reports and did not respond to the BBC’s request for comment.

The database is the National Crime Information Center (NCIC). Federal and local law enforcement agencies use it to share information about arrest warrants and background checks. Police officers also access it during traffic stops and investigations. According to the FBI, as of 2023, the NCIC contained more than 18 million active records across 22 databases and provided services to over 100,000 law enforcement and criminal justice organisations.

Reports say the intrusion was found in recent days, and nobody has said when it happened, how the attackers got in, who they are, or whether they took anything. It’s also unclear whether the incident disrupted police access to the system.

Bureau officials learned of it on Thursday, according to CNN.


President Donald Trump briefly commented on the incident during a Fox News interview on Saturday. He said he had just learned about the breach, called it bad news and said he did not like it. He also suggested that the investigation might reveal information that officials would not otherwise have discovered.

“But maybe we’ll learn things that we would’ve never learned otherwise,” Trump said.

On Sunday, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told Fox News that the FBI was investigating who was behind the incident. However, he did not share further details about the intrusion.

The incident comes during a difficult week for US technology and government services. Several outages affected banking, air traffic control and other sectors. Officials say these disruptions were not caused by cyberattacks, although they have attracted the attention of lawmakers.

It’s also not the first time the FBI suffered a cyber attack, in September, the ShinyHunters crime group claimed it had stolen sensitive information on all bureau staff, around 38,000 people. ShinyHunters provided a possible technical explanation for the alleged intrusion. The group claims the exploitation of an Oracle PeopleSoft zero-day, reportedly using it to gain remote code execution through infrastructure connected to the FBI’s recruitment services.

item.title: U.S. CISA adds N-able MailAssure and Project MONAI flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog
item.description:
U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) adds N-able MailAssure and Project MONAI flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added N-able MailAssure and Project MONAI vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog:

  • CVE-2026-133968 Project MONAI MONAI Label Path Traversal Vulnerability
  • CVE-2026-134624 N-able Mail Assure (SpamExperts) Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Vulnerability

The first flaw is CVE-2026-133968 (CVSS score of 9.8), a critical path traversal vulnerability in Project MONAI’s MONAI Label. It affects versions up to 0.8.5 and allows unauthenticated remote attackers to access files outside the intended directory through the image parameter in the PUT /datastore/image endpoint. Successful exploitation can also lead to remote code execution, potentially allowing attackers to take control of the affected server. The vulnerability has been exploited in the wild since September 2026, before its public disclosure on November 20.

Amazon Threat Intelligence linked the exploitation to a Chinese-nexus threat actor, with moderate confidence. According to Amazon, the attackers used autonomous AI agents running the open-source Cairn framework to discover and exploit the zero-day. The agents reportedly gained root access to a university server and later used the vulnerability to target another university network. Amazon has not identified a specific threat group. The vulnerability was fixed in MONAI Label 0.8.6.

The second flaw is CVE-2026-134624 (CVSS score of 9.3), a critical Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in N-able Mail Assure (SpamExperts). The flaw affects versions earlier than 20261121.1943 and exists in the LDAP synchronisation connection check performed when a relay is configured. It does not properly restrict the destination of the connection, allowing an authenticated API user with sufficient privileges to make the vulnerable server connect to arbitrary internal IP addresses and ports. Attackers could use this capability to identify accessible internal systems and send crafted requests to internal services. N-able

N-able disclosed the vulnerability while investigating a cyberattack against its Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud environments. The company confirmed that attackers had accessed a web server and said its investigation had found no evidence of exploitation beyond a single N-able-hosted server. However, it has not confirmed whether CVE-2026-134624 was the vulnerability exploited to gain initial access. No threat actor has been publicly identified. The flaw was fixed in version 20261121.1943, and N-able restored access to the affected services on November 21, 2026.

According to Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 22-01: Reducing the Significant Risk of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities, FCEB agencies have to address the identified vulnerabilities by the due date to protect their networks against attacks exploiting the flaws in the catalog.

Experts also recommend that private organizations review the Catalog and address the vulnerabilities in their infrastructure.

CISA orders federal agencies to fix the vulnerabilities by November 26.

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, CISA)

item.title: EU Academy Users’ Names and Emails Exposed in EU Commission Hack
item.description:
The EU Commission confirms an AI-powered cyberattack leaked EU Academy users’ names and emails. China-backed threat actors are suspected.

The European Commission has confirmed that the cyberattack it disclosed last week exposed personal data.

The European Commission (EC) confirmed that the cyberattack exposed personal information.

When the attack was discovered, several applications were temporarily shut down. At the time, the Commission said it had found no evidence that staff data had been compromised. EU cybersecurity experts have still not confirmed that any staff data was stolen, but the attack affected another group of users.

On Monday, Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier told reporters that the investigation had uncovered a data breach involving EU Academy. The platform offers online courses about EU policies to people outside the Commission. According to Euronews, it also provides professional training and specialised learning opportunities for young people.

What was taken is limited so far, but the picture isn’t final. Compromised information includes names and email addresses of EU Academy users. Access to the platform is suspended, and the European Data Protection Supervisor has been notified.

“The Commission has confirmed a leak of names and email addresses and is warning users of possible follow-ups from the attacker, such as phishing campaigns based on their personal data.” Euronews reports.

“That is the first major consequence of the incident. For other IT systems, EU cyber experts have not confirmed data theft affecting Commission staff, though several internal apps were taken offline as a precaution and some remain unavailable.”

Regnier said the scale of the leak is still under investigation, so the Commission posted one general message for everyone on the website, out of transparency, instead of contacting individuals.

CERT-EU, the cybersecurity team that protects EU institutions, detected the activity on 22 October and identified ARTEX, an AI-powered penetration-testing tool, as a possible tool used in the attack. An EU official told Politico that some threat actors misuse tools like ARTEX and have targeted the Commission. In a technical note published on 5 November, CERT-EU described ARTEX as a system that uses AI agents. An operator gives it an objective in plain language, and the software breaks it down into smaller tasks that the agents carry out using real hacking tools.

Last week EU experts said the attack had largely been contained, but Euronews tells a different story:

“On 22 October, the Commission’s IT department detected a malicious actor in its internal networks.” states euroNews. “A month after the attack began, the EU executive has yet to fully contain the breach and was forced to take the EU Academy website offline on Saturday.”

Regnier wouldn’t say on Monday whether the incident is over. Euronews’ sources describe an attack that’s still moving through Commission IT systems. Several internal apps were taken offline as a precaution, and some remain unavailable.

At this time, nobody has linked the attack to a specific actor, because Regnier said attribution has to wait until the investigation ends.

Euronews reports, citing two sources familiar with the matter, that the European Commission suspects a China-backed group of hackers is behind the large-scale cyberattack. The attack is reportedly still spreading through the Commission’s IT systems.

Inside the Commission, the suspected attackers are reportedly referred to as “Panda”. The term is used by the cybersecurity industry to loosely link threat actors to China. However, no official source has confirmed this attribution publicly.

The suspicion is based on the attack’s level of sophistication and the reported use of ARTEX, a Chinese-developed tool that uses AI to find vulnerabilities that attackers can exploit.

Euronews says Microsoft and CrowdStrike have tied ARTEX-driven espionage campaigns against hundreds of organisations to China-linked groups they call Storm-0940 and Panda Vapor.

The current threat assessment says the actor wasn’t going after specific systems or people. It wanted to test how far it could get into the Commission’s networks. A narrower target would have called for a quieter attack.

The Commission’s handling of the breach upset its staff union, which says employees learned about it from the press. The Commission also says public disclosure may alert attackers to its response and cause panic too. For EU Academy users, the risk is phishing: stolen names and email addresses could make scam messages more convincing. Users should be cautious with unexpected messages, visit the Academy website directly, and avoid sharing personal information with anyone claiming to represent the Commission.

This isn’t the Commission’s first hit this year. On March 24, the European Commission detected a cyberattack affecting the cloud infrastructure hosting its Europa.eu websites. The incident was quickly contained, with mitigation measures applied and no disruption to website availability. CERT-EU attributed a European Commission cloud breach to the TeamPCP threat group, revealing that data from at least 30 EU entities was exposed.

TeamPCP reportedly accessed the EU’s AWS environment on March 10 using a stolen API key from the Trivy supply-chain attack.

They then used tools like TruffleHog to find more credentials, created new access keys to stay hidden, and carried out reconnaissance and data theft. TeamPCP is also linked to supply-chain attacks on platforms like GitHub, PyPI, NPM, and Docker, including a compromised LiteLLM package used to spread data-stealing malware.

On 30 January, the European Commission detected another cyberattack that hit its mobile device management system. The organization pointed out that no mobile devices were compromised. The Commission contained and cleaned the system within nine hours. 

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, EU Commission)

item.title: VMware patches critical vCenter authentication bypass and ESX flaws
item.description:
Broadcom patches 23 VMware flaws, including a critical vCenter authentication bypass and three flaws allowing code execution on ESX hosts.

Broadcom has released security updates to address 23 vulnerabilities affecting multiple VMware products, including vCenter, ESX, Workstation, Fusion, VMware Tools, and Avi Load Balancer. The security advisory includes four critical-severity flaws, with the most serious tracked as CVE-2026-123903 (CVSS score of 9.8).

This vulnerability affects the VMware Directory Service (vmdir) in vCenter. An attacker with network access to a vulnerable server could exploit the flaw to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access.

Broadcom published the issue in its security advisory VMSA-2026-0011. The company credited researchers from Qianxin, depthfirst, and ThreatBook for independently reporting the vulnerability.

The new flaw is distinct from CVE-2026-123890, the authentication bypass disclosed on November 19. Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant reported that the suspected Chinese espionage group tracked as ARMORY CASTLE (formerly UNC5221) had exploited the earlier vulnerability since September 2026.

According to Mandiant, the attackers used a custom tool called BONESAW to exploit vCenter, obtain an administrator session, steal sensitive data, and create a new SSO administrator account. They subsequently used additional tools to forge authentication tokens and maintain access to compromised environments.

Broadcom’s latest advisory also addresses several other vCenter vulnerabilities. CVE-2026-123904 (CVSS score of 7.5) is an arbitrary file write flaw affecting archive processing. An attacker with access to the backup repository could write files to arbitrary locations with root privileges, potentially leading to code execution on the appliance.

Three other vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-123905, CVE-2026-123906, and CVE-2026-123907, could allow attackers with network access to disrupt the VMware Directory Service and make it unavailable.

The ESX updates fix several other serious flaws. Two critical vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-123910 and CVE-2026-123911, both have a CVSS score of 9.8 and affect the I/O filter service. One can cause an out-of-bounds write in the heap, while the other is a use-after-free flaw. An attacker with network access could exploit either vulnerability to execute code on the ESX host.

Another critical vulnerability, CVE-2026-123912 (CVSS 9.3), affects the XHCI USB controller in ESX, VMware Workstation, and Fusion. Exploiting it requires local administrator privileges inside a virtual machine and could allow an attacker to run code as the VMX process. On ESX, this code remains restricted to the VMX sandbox. On Workstation and Fusion, however, it could lead to code execution on the host machine.

The advisory also covers eight vulnerabilities in Avi Load Balancer and a denial-of-service issue in VMware Tools.

Broadcom has released patches for the affected products. The fixes for vCenter are available in version 9.1.2 for the 9.1 branch, 9.0.2.0300 for the 9.0 branch, and 8.0 U3m for vCenter 8.0. Organizations running vCenter 7.0 should contact Broadcom Support if they have an extended support contract.

The company also published fixes for ESX, Workstation, Fusion, VMware Tools, and Avi Load Balancer. Administrators should consult the official Broadcom advisory for the complete list of affected versions and corresponding updates.

The rapid succession of critical vCenter disclosures, including a vulnerability already exploited in targeted attacks, makes patch management and restricting network access to management interfaces particularly important for organizations relying on VMware infrastructure.

item.title: Maritime industry faces growing cyber threats as 50 ships targeted
item.description:
US authorities investigate suspected cyberattacks on up to 50 commercial ships, with Iran and Russia under scrutiny and Fortinet flaws involved.

The United States is investigating a wave of cyberattacks targeting commercial vessels carrying oil, liquefied petroleum gas, chemicals, and other potentially hazardous cargo. According to a Wall Street Journal report, as many as 50 ships may have been targeted, with Iran emerging as the primary suspect.

“The U.S. is investigating Iran’s potential involvement in dozens of cyberattacks against energy tankers amid concerns that Tehran is widening the war with cyber operations and terror plots against Americans far from the Middle East.” WSJ states.

“As many as 50 ships carrying oil, liquefied petroleum, chemical products and other explosive substances are believed to have been attacked, according to U.S. officials and others familiar with the matter.”

US authorities are also considering possible Russian involvement. However, a Trump administration official told the WSJ that investigators have found no evidence linking Iran to the incidents and described four of the attacks as minor disruptions.

The incidents reportedly involved both cyber intrusions and intimidation campaigns. Some vessels received bomb threats, ransom demands, and messages warning them against transporting US products. Other ships may have been compromised without their crews being aware of the intrusions.

The US Coast Guard has reportedly deployed specialized cyber protection teams to at least four vessels approaching US ports to investigate and mitigate potential threats. The VL Prosperity and Kohaku were among the ships inspected after suspected compromises of their onboard networks.

The attackers are reportedly exploiting vulnerabilities in Fortinet networking devices widely used across the maritime industry. In September, the US Coast Guard Cyber Command and the FBI issued a joint alert warning shipping companies about state-sponsored actors exploiting FortiGate vulnerabilities in maritime environments.

The investigation also concerns vessels operating near Europe and Asia. One of them, the Vivit Africa LNG carrier, was reportedly targeted while transporting liquefied natural gas from the United States to Italy. The vessel experienced onboard system problems and received a bomb threat, although publicly available information does not establish that a cyberattack caused the technical incident.

The incidents highlight the growing exposure of commercial shipping to cyber threats. Modern vessels rely on interconnected IT and operational technology (OT) systems to manage communications, navigation, and cargo operations. A compromise of onboard networks could disrupt operations, delay deliveries, and create safety concerns, although the reported incidents do not demonstrate that attackers gained control of critical navigation or propulsion systems.

Alon Ayalon, co-founder of maritime cybersecurity firm Cydome, told the WSJ that most vessels have “less cyber protection than a midsize office.”

Even without causing physical damage, cyber intrusions and threats can force shipping companies to suspend operations, undergo security inspections, and face costly delays. The investigation highlights the need for maritime operators to address exposed network devices, strengthen remote access controls, and improve the separation between IT and OT environments.

item.title: GT13: AI-Assisted Hackers Target 22 Organizations Through Check Point Servers
item.description:
GreyNoise tracks GT13, an unattributed, probably AI-assisted campaign that hit 22 organizations via Check Point management servers. It may still be running.

GreyNoise detailed an intrusion campaign against Check Point Security Management Servers. The company confirmed attacks between October 17 and November 2, 2026, and counts at least 22 victim organizations. It tracks the activity as GreyNoise Threat 13, or GT13.

“GreyNoise recently discovered an intrusion campaign targeting Check Point Security Management Servers, with confirmed attack activity between October 17th and November 2nd, 2026, impacting at least 22 distinct organizations globally.” reads the report published by GreyNoise.

The victims don’t share a country or an industry. They have assets in the United Kingdom, Ireland, France, the Netherlands, Greece, Germany, Austria, Bulgaria, Poland, India, Thailand, Vietnam, South Korea, Hong Kong, China, Australia and the United States. The sectors include financial services, energy, government, transportation, mining, engineering and manufacturing.

GreyNoise cannot attribute the campaign to any known or publicly tracked threat group. The company also says it lacks enough information to identify the attackers’ motives or country of origin.

GreyNoise tracked most of the activity through its Global Observation Grid, a network of sensors designed to attract and monitor scanning and exploitation attempts. These sensors work much like honeypots, but the company says they offer broader coverage. They allow researchers to observe entire attacks as they happen, rather than relying only on reports from victims.

The attackers used 99 IP addresses, many of them temporary. These addresses belonged either to ExpressVPN exit nodes or to compromised Check Point devices. GreyNoise recorded more than 1,400 network sessions, 800 command-line artifacts, and 1,200 files that were downloaded, uploaded, or created.

The part GreyNoise saw begins with a file server. On October 2 at 13:17 UTC, the actor started scanning and attacking a Rejetto HFS server through CVE-2026-61500. Every POST to the loginSrp1 endpoint returns a signed session cookie that holds a “sid” value drawn from JavaScript’s Math.random() function.

After several logins in a row, the actor had enough output to rebuild the internal state of the V8 random number generator. That gave it the key that signs session cookies, so it could forge an admin cookie and log in without a password. Two minutes later, GreyNoise saw admin requests carrying forged cookies, and the server hadn’t been patched.

The forged cookie also carried “allow_session_ip_change:true”, which lets it work from any IP address. GreyNoise calls that perfect for an attacker behind a VPN or hopping between exits. On October 5, the actor used the same trick to install HFS middleware hooks that run commands, and it added an SSH key to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys.

On October 8, the attacker’s automated system ran a few basic commands to check the system, available disk space, and current user. The activity then stopped until October 19. On that day, the attackers used forged session cookies and the HFS server_code feature to try to download a Linux implant called “ZULT”. They did this despite already having SSH access to the server.

The download failed. The attackers checked running processes, tested the download link with curl, and inspected the network settings. They could not work out why the implant had failed to download, so they returned the next day and used a direct SSH connection to continue setting up their relay. GreyNoise believes this failure may point to problems in a multi-agent system, suggesting that even automated tools can run into issues.

On October 20, the attackers created a script to start an HTTP server on the compromised machine without requiring authentication. They then began uploading files. The first archive contained the results of a network route scan from a Check Point Security Management Server, showing that the attackers had already gained access to that system. They then installed Nmap and Chisel and configured Chisel to work as a reverse proxy.

That made the HFS server a relay, or “hop” in GreyNoise’s wording. The actor used it to run its operations against Check Point devices it had compromised earlier, and to store the results. GreyNoise couldn’t determine when or how the actor got into those Check Point systems, only that it was there before the HFS compromise.

Between October 20 and 26, the actor had a compromised machine in one victim’s network, which GreyNoise calls Victim A, download Chisel and run it as a client. Through that tunnel, a script for CVE-2026-16232 (a Check Point SmartConsole authentication bypass that leads to Run Script) launched more than 100 management tasks on several management servers. The tasks copied the firewall database and the internal certificate authority, minted a new certificate called pivot.p12, and unloaded security policies, which would switch the firewall off.

The actor also probed Citrix NetScaler, Ivanti Connect Secure, VMware vCenter, Microsoft Exchange, Oracle TNS and several domain controllers. It ran exploits for CVE-2020-1472 (Netlogon), CVE-2023-4966 (NetScaler), CVE-2024-21893 (Ivanti), CVE-2021-26855 and CVE-2021-34473 (Exchange), and CVE-2021-21972 and CVE-2023-34048 (vCenter). GreyNoise also lists CVE-2025-5777, CVE-2026-41089 and CVE-2026-98432 among the flaws the actor used or tried to use.

“The actor used Nmap, Chisel, Impacket, Paramiko and other Python tooling to perform intrusion activities against their victim assets, including attempts to perform internal reconnaissance, privilege escalation, and lateral movement.” continues the report. “The bulk of the adversary commands and interaction is too voluminous to dig into here, but we can expose some of the adversary’s TTPs by taking a glimpse at their tooling. The actor used at least 30 Python scripts, many of which were helpers or launchers for other scripts, and several of them were probes for vulnerabilities or runners of exploits. Excerpts are provided below to illustrate the more specialized tooling and workflows.”

Password guessing played a part too. Scripts named spray_portal.py, comb.py, ssh_comb.py and ssh_spray.py carried common, default and weak passwords, plus usernames and passwords themed to the victim. The actor either knew its target or guessed well.

When a second Check Point server wouldn’t report back to the hop, the actor wrote a pull script to steal its data through the first server. The script harvested credentials, internal CA files and the firewall configuration. It was named after the targeted device.

On October 26 at 02:17 UTC, a bulk certificate task went out to 24 compromised Check Point servers: Victim A’s and those of 21 other victims. Results came back to the hop as text files that listed victim IP addresses in increasing order, so a loop was clearly running through them. GreyNoise never saw the actor send the task, which points to another part of its infrastructure.

Every file showed an error, because the certificate task had failed. One message also flagged a preload error for /usr/lib/.libproc.so, registered in /etc/ld.so.preload, which may indicate an implant. GreyNoise saw no follow-up attempts, but the IP addresses in those files let it notify many victims, directly or through government partners.

Check Point’s position, as reported by The Hacker News, is that this isn’t a new weakness. Sergey Shykevich, its director of threat intelligence, said the activity “does not represent a new vulnerability or exploitation technique”, since CVE-2026-16232 was disclosed earlier and patches exist. The company wants customers to apply updates, follow its hardening guidance to restrict management access and look for suspicious activity.

By early November, other attackers had started scanning the hop and trying to abuse it. On November 2 at 02:28 UTC, the GT13 actor ran a script that checked the box for CVE-2026-98432, a Linux IPv4 use-after-free bug. It then used nftables to drop IPv4 packets with IP options that could trigger the flaw. The attacker did patch management on its relay, which is more than some victims managed.

GreyNoise doesn’t read much into the clock. It saw no hands-on-keyboard activity between roughly 17:00 and 00:19 UTC, and nothing in the 05:00 hour, which fits a UTC+7 or UTC+8 workday. The malware domain newpayapp[.]com was registered on March 13, 2026, with the registrant state “Hai Phong” and country code “VN”, and GreyNoise treats that as a possible coincidence. The infrastructure clearly existed long before anyone noticed it.

GreyNoise believes GT13 used AI tools to find vulnerable systems, develop exploits and automate attacks, although human operators were also involved. The company is sharing information with authorities and CERTs. Its monitoring stopped on November 2, but it warns that the campaign may still be active because attackers retain access to compromised Check Point devices.

“We suspect the GT13 actor has a mature AI-enabled offensive apparatus. We believe the actor has separate agentic harnesses and systems weaponizing vulnerabilities, scanning for vulnerable assets, and automatically exploiting them to gather sets of systems that can be later used for operational relays or true targets.” concludes the report. “We suspect some of the foibles in the timeline reflect agentic offensive operations.”

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Check Point)

item.title: U.S. CISA adds Drupal Core, Idunno AntiCsrf, and Optimizely Web Experimentation flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog
item.description:
U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) adds Drupal Core, Idunno AntiCsrf, and Optimizely Web Experimentation flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added Drupal Core, Idunno AntiCsrf, and Optimizely Web Experimentation vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog:

  • CVE-2026-131914 Idunno AntiCsrf Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability 
  • CVE-2026-132165 Drupal Core Remote Code Execution Vulnerability 
  • CVE-2026-132224 Optimizely Web Experimentation External Control of Critical State Data Vulnerability 

The first flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-131914 (CVSS score of 9.8), is a critical insecure deserialization vulnerability affecting Idunno AntiCsrf, a legacy ASP.NET library used to protect web applications against Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) attacks. The vulnerability allows unauthenticated remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on vulnerable servers by sending a specially crafted HTTP POST request. Mandiant confirmed that the flaw is being actively exploited in the wild. However, the security firm has not attributed the attacks to any specific threat actor. The affected library is no longer maintained, and no official security patch is available. Organizations are advised to remove it and replace it with a supported anti-CSRF solution.

item.title: Electrolux Smart Boilers in Ukraine Connect to Russian Servers, Raising Privacy Concerns
item.description:
Researchers found Electrolux-branded smart boilers connecting to Russian servers, raising concerns about household data and privacy.

A router in Ukraine recorded a water heater doing something odd. The owner, Alexander Unger, saw his Electrolux EWH 80 look up a server called mqtt.cloud.rusklimat.ru and then try to connect to it. He published the records on Facebook, including a lookup timed at 18:00 on November 23, 2026.

Mysterium VPN’s research team checked the finding. They repeated the lookup on November 25 and got the same address, 130.193.49[.]173. RIPE, the registry for Europe and Russia, lists that block under Yandex.Cloud LLC at 16 Lva Tolstogo Street in Moscow.

The server belongs to Rusklimat, a Moscow group that calls itself the leader of Russia’s climate-equipment market. Its Hommyn app uses that name to reach heaters, air conditioners and ventilation units. Developers who link such devices to Home Assistant list it as the official cloud for Ballu, Electrolux, Zanussi and Royal Thermo, and a 2025 guide on Habr says the devices contact it by default.

Rusklimat sells Electrolux-branded boilers in Russia and advertises them for Hommyn and for Yandex’s voice assistant, Alisa. Mysterium adds, citing Meduza, that Ukraine struck three of Yandex’s six data centers in October 2026 and disrupted Yandex Cloud, where Rusklimat’s server runs.

“The manual for the EWH SI EEC series, hosted by the Austrian arm of the home-improvement chain Hornbach, names CladSwiss AG of Zug, Switzerland, as the manufacturer and says the boiler is made in China. It says the Electrolux name is used under license from AB Electrolux, the Swedish parent company.” reads the report published by Mysterium. “It adds that the remote-control app, ClimatOn, comes from CladSwiss and isn’t provided by Electrolux.”

The manual also says the Electrolux name is used under license from AB Electrolux of Sweden, and that the remote-control app, ClimatOn, comes from CladSwiss, not Electrolux. Retailers lean on the Swedish angle: Rozetka gives Sweden as the country of brand registration, and the series is sold in Serbia, Poland and Lithuania.

This single appliance has links to five countries: Sweden, Switzerland, China, Germany, and Russia. That’s quite a complicated background for a water heater installed in someone’s bathroom.

According to CladSwiss, the data collected by its ClimatOn app should be stored in Frankfurt, Germany. Mysterium also found a ClimatOn server hosted on Amazon infrastructure in Germany. This means the boiler can connect to two different servers, depending on which app the owner uses.

Both apps use the same technology platform. A developer who created software to control an Electrolux SmartInverter boiler locally found that the device identifies itself on the home network as a Syncleo device. Syncleo is based in Israel, has an office in Russia, and lists Rusklimat among its customers.

Why did a buyer in Ukraine end up on the Russian app? Mysterium doesn’t know. Unger, it was told, set the boiler up with Hommyn, and a buyer of another Electrolux model wrote on Rozetka in June 2026 that the Wi-Fi worked properly only through the Russian app. Mysterium has asked CladSwiss which app buyers in Ukraine and the EU are pointed to.

The Russian app knows this boiler by name. Its Google Play page shows an “Electrolux SmartInverter” in the first screenshot, and version 1.20.2 of the Android app lists 118 devices, 19 of them Electrolux, including the series named in the manual. Its privacy policy names R-Klimat LLC of Moscow as the operator and says personal data stays “exclusively within the territory” of Russia, under Russian law.

“The privacy policy bundled in the app names R-Klimat LLC of Moscow as the operator and says the app stores users’ personal information “exclusively within the territory” of Russia, under Russian law. The app is written to send sign-in details (a phone number or email address) and the name and room of each device to Rusklimat servers. It keeps device history on Yandex Cloud and sends the phone’s location to a Hommyn weather service.” continues the report. “The app also carries one fixed username and password for Rusklimat’s device server, the same in every copy. We didn’t use them and are not publishing them.”

Mysterium didn’t use the credentials and won’t publish them. Neither will I.

The brand’s website points the same way. English manuals send buyers to home-comfort.com, which gives CladSwiss, at an address in Baar, Switzerland, as its contact. Its contact form asks visitors, in Russian, to let a company called RK-Region process their data under Russian federal law 152-FZ. Rusklimat’s shop names RK-Region in its payment details, and ballu.ru carries the same consent text.

Swiss register data show CladSwiss was entered in December 2019 to trade technical equipment, especially air-conditioning units. Mysterium found nothing that shows who owns the company or how it connects to Rusklimat beyond these records.

What can the server see? CladSwiss’s Data Act declaration lists whether a device is on, its temperature, its operating mode and its power level, about 1 MB a day on standby and 3 MB in use. The privacy policy adds the phone’s identifier, its IP address and the names of Wi-Fi networks, plus location if the user agrees.

“A record of when a household heats water shows when people are at home. The line that carries those reports also carries commands to switch the boiler on or change its temperature. For a boiler tied to mqtt.cloud.rusklimat.ru, that line ends at a Russian company’s server in Moscow.” Mysterium states. “Russia isn’t among the countries the European Commission recognizes as protecting personal data adequately, and Ukraine first ordered its internet providers to block Yandex’s services in 2017.”

The same line also carries commands to switch the boiler on or change its temperature. Mysterium notes that Russia isn’t among the countries the European Commission recognizes as protecting personal data adequately.

One claim remains untested. Developers who studied a Ballu ventilation unit from the same family wrote that every unit shipped with the same cloud login and didn’t check the server’s certificate. Mysterium hasn’t tested that and doesn’t know whether it applies to the boiler.

Mysterium sent questions to AB Electrolux, CladSwiss and Rozetka on November 25, and none had replied at publication. AB Electrolux sold its Russian business in 2022 and said then that it had no production in Russia and wouldn’t supply the company it sold. Rusklimat’s Russian shop sells heaters under the Electrolux name today.

Mysterium stresses that its findings are limited. Researchers did not connect to the servers or examine the boiler itself. They only reviewed the Hommyn app’s code, so they cannot confirm what data the device actually sends.

Users can check their router logs for connections to “rusklimat” or use DNS monitoring tools such as Pi-hole, AdGuard Home or NextDNS. Blocking the Russian server stops remote access, although local control may still work over Wi-Fi. Users can also disable the boiler’s Wi-Fi and place smart appliances on a separate guest network to keep them away from computers and phones. These checks also apply to Hommyn and ClimatOn devices from Ballu and Zanussi.

“A VPN on your phone or laptop doesn’t change where an appliance on your Wi-Fi sends its data, so the fix here sits at the router.” concludes the report.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Electrolux Smart Boilers)
